result.title: Curriculum unlearning in humans and neural networks
result.summary: During learning, humans often benefit from curricula that teach simple rules before exceptions. However, we lack a computational explanation for this phenomenon. Here, using a canonical behavioural task and modelling with neural networks, we develop and test a theory for why simple-to-complex curricula succeed. We show that during learning, both humans and neural networks show simplicity biases, a tendency to learn simple rules that are underfit to the data. In neural networks this bias is accompanied by compression of neural representations. Simple-to-complex curricula help both types of learners overcome this compression, developing representations (and policy) with appropriate dimensionality for the task. We test and confirm a further prediction from this theory: learners that have been pre-exposed to simple tasks and with more compressed initial representations benefit more from curricula. These findings suggest that curricula help with ``unlearning'' of simple rules.

AI.brief_summary: 该文用经典行为任务与神经网络建模，提出并检验「由简到繁」课程为何有效：人类与网络都表现出对简单规则的欠拟合偏置，并伴随神经表示压缩，课程帮助学习者「反学习」简单规则、形成与任务匹配的表示维度。
AI.relevance_reason: 其「简单性偏置—表示压缩—维度适配」框架可能为 LVR 中 latent 状态信息坍缩、任务必要信息是否保留及课程式训练监督提供启发线索，但该文并非视觉或多模态推理研究，迁移需核查。
